categories.categoryDescription: Career statistics and performance metrics for fantasy managers

metrics.shortDescription: Composite score ranking managers for Hall of Fame consideration
metrics.detailedDescription: A weighted combination of championships and career win rate. Titles carry most of the weight and are measured against the most titles any manager has won, so every score is relative to the league's title leader.
metrics.calculationFormula: (Championships ÷ Max Championships × 0.6) + (Win Percentage × 0.4)
metrics.exampleCalculation: Manager with 2 championships (max=3) and 65% win rate: (2÷3 × 0.6) + (0.65 × 0.4) = 0.660
metrics.interpretationGuide: Higher is better. 1.000 would take the most titles in league history and a perfect record, so only the league's title leader gets near the top of the scale. Titles carry 60% of the weight: one championship moves the index more than several winning seasons. Tiers go by score: 0.600 and up is Hall of Fame Elite, 0.400 Hall of Fame, 0.250 Hall of Very Good, and anything lower Solid Contributor.
metrics.limitations: Only managers with at least three seasons are ranked at all, so newer managers are absent rather than scored low. Championships are divided by the current league maximum, so every new title rescales the metric and a score from one year is not comparable to a score from another. A title and a regular season win rate are weighted the same regardless of league size, schedule strength or era.

metrics.shortDescription: Percentage of games won over entire fantasy career
metrics.detailedDescription: The proportion of total games won including ties (counted as half wins). This is the primary measure of sustained success in fantasy football.
metrics.calculationFormula: (Total Wins + 0.5 × Total Ties) ÷ Total Games Played
metrics.exampleCalculation: Manager with 45 wins, 2 ties, 35 losses: (45 + 0.5×2) ÷ 82 = 56.1%
metrics.interpretationGuide: Industry benchmarks: 60%+ is excellent, 55%+ is very good, 50%+ is above average, below 45% indicates struggles.
metrics.limitations: Ties count as half a win here, but the manager analytics path computes the same field without that adjustment, so the two can disagree for managers who have tied. Every game across twenty seasons is weighted equally despite changes in league size, roster rules and scoring settings.

metrics.shortDescription: A badge for the titles a manager has won.
metrics.detailedDescription: Named for the number of championships a manager has won in their career.
metrics.calculationFormula: 3 or more titles: Dynasty builder. 2: Repeat champion. 1: Champion.
metrics.exampleCalculation: A manager with 7 titles: Dynasty builder
metrics.interpretationGuide: No badge until a manager wins a title.

metrics.shortDescription: A badge for how much a manager scores per game over their career.
metrics.detailedDescription: Named for a manager's career points per game, regular season and playoffs.
metrics.calculationFormula: 130 or more points per game: Offensive powerhouse. 120 or more: High scorer.
metrics.exampleCalculation: A manager averaging 129.1 points per game: High scorer
metrics.interpretationGuide: No badge below 120 points per game.

metrics.shortDescription: A badge for a manager's career win rate.
metrics.detailedDescription: Named for a manager's career win rate, ties counted as half a win.
metrics.calculationFormula: A win rate of .700 or better: Dominance. .600 or better: Consistent winner. .500 or better: Above average.
metrics.exampleCalculation: A manager winning .563 of their games: Above average
metrics.interpretationGuide: No badge below .500.

metrics.shortDescription: A badge for how many seasons a manager has played.
metrics.detailedDescription: Named for the number of seasons a manager has played in the league.
metrics.calculationFormula: 15 or more seasons: League veteran. 10 or more: Long timer. 5 or more: Established. Fewer: Newcomer.
metrics.exampleCalculation: A manager in their 22nd season: League veteran
metrics.interpretationGuide: Every manager has one; it only counts seasons, not results.

categories.categoryDescription: Season and weekly team performance metrics

metrics.shortDescription: Composite team strength rating based on multiple performance factors
metrics.detailedDescription: Combines record, point differential, strength of schedule, and recent form into a single team rating.
metrics.calculationFormula: (Win% × 0.4) + (Points ÷ Best Points That Week × 0.3) + (Recent Form ÷ Best Form That Week × 0.2) + ((1 − Strength of Schedule) × 0.1)
metrics.exampleCalculation: Team at 70% wins, 90% of the week's top score, 80% of the top recent form, 0.55 SOS: (0.70×0.4) + (0.90×0.3) + (0.80×0.2) + (0.45×0.1) = 0.755
metrics.interpretationGuide: Runs 0 to 1 and is relative to the rest of the league that week. Observed league history: 0.65 is average, 0.75+ is a strong week, above 0.85 is dominant, below 0.45 is struggling.
metrics.limitations: Points and recent form are normalised against the best team in that same league week, so the score describes standing relative to the field at that moment and cannot be compared across weeks or seasons. Where strength of schedule is missing it defaults to 0.5, which quietly pushes the schedule term to neutral rather than flagging the gap.

metrics.shortDescription: Difficulty rating of opponents faced based on their performance
metrics.detailedDescription: The average win percentage of every opponent a team has faced. A value above 0.500 means the team drew opponents who were better than a coin flip against the rest of the league.
metrics.calculationFormula: Average of (Opponent Win Percentage) across all games played
metrics.interpretationGuide: Centred on 0.500 by construction. 0.550+ is a hard schedule, 0.450-0.550 is ordinary, below 0.450 is soft.
metrics.limitations: Averaging opponents' win percentages is circular: beating your opponents lowers their win percentage and therefore lowers your own strength of schedule. Weeks with no matched opponent default to 0.500, so a team with missing games drifts toward average rather than showing a gap.

categories.categoryDescription: Metrics measuring how competitive and balanced a league is

metrics.shortDescription: Overall measure of how competitive and balanced a league is
metrics.detailedDescription: Composite score combining win percentage parity, point spread tightness, playoff race drama, and frequency of close games. Higher scores indicate more competitive leagues.
metrics.calculationFormula: 0.25×(Win Parity Score) + 0.25×(Point Spread Score) + 0.25×(Playoff Race Score) + 0.25×(Close Games Score)
metrics.interpretationGuide: Higher is more competitive. Across this league's 21 seasons the index has run 39.0 to 65.9 with a mean of 56.3, so 60+ is a genuinely tight year and below 50 is a season somebody ran away with.
metrics.limitations: The four components are weighted equally by choice, not because the data says they matter equally. Two of them floor at zero, so leagues past that point cannot be told apart. The playoff race component counts teams within one game of the last playoff spot and scales at ten points per team, which assumes a ten team league.

metrics.shortDescription: Measures how evenly distributed wins are across teams
metrics.detailedDescription: Component of competitiveness measuring win percentage equality. Calculated as 100 minus the standard deviation of win percentages scaled by 300.
metrics.calculationFormula: 100 - (Standard Deviation of Win Percentages × 300)
metrics.exampleCalculation: League where win% ranges from 40-70% (StdDev=8.2%): 100 - (0.082×300) = 75.4
metrics.interpretationGuide: Higher is better: 85+ indicates very balanced competition, 70-85 is good parity, below 70 suggests dominant teams.
metrics.limitations: The ×300 scale factor is arbitrary, picked to put ordinary leagues in a readable range. The floor at zero means any league with a win percentage spread beyond roughly a third cannot be distinguished from a worse one. It says nothing about whether the same team wins every year, only about how one season's wins were spread.

metrics.shortDescription: Measures how tightly grouped team point totals are
metrics.detailedDescription: Component of competitiveness measuring scoring equality. Calculated as 100 minus the relative point spread between highest and lowest scoring teams.
metrics.calculationFormula: 100 - ((Max Points - Min Points) ÷ Average Points × 100)
metrics.interpretationGuide: Higher indicates closer scoring: 80+ is very tight, 65-80 is competitive, below 65 suggests big scoring gaps.
metrics.limitations: Uses only the highest and lowest scoring teams, so one outlier sets the score and the shape of the middle is invisible. Like win parity it floors at zero once the spread exceeds the league average.

metrics.shortDescription: Expected wins based on points scored vs points allowed
metrics.detailedDescription: Estimates how many regular-season games a team "should have" won from points scored and allowed alone. The exponent is fitted to this league's own completed seasons rather than borrowed from another sport.
metrics.calculationFormula: Points For^x ÷ (Points For^x + Points Against^x) × Games Played, with x fitted to league history (6.26 through 2025)
metrics.interpretationGuide: Compare with regular-season wins. A record more than about a game and a half from this, either way, is unusual in a single season; over a career it should come close to even.
metrics.limitations: The exponent is one number for the whole league across twenty years, refitted only when a season finishes. It describes a season well (it is fitted to describe) but predicts badly: from the first seven weeks, Pythagorean win percentage at 6.26 forecasts the rest of the season worse than a plain .500 guess, because early-season scoring is noisy. It assumes points scored and allowed are independent, which head-to-head scheduling breaks.

metrics.shortDescription: Difference between actual wins and expected wins (Pythagorean)
metrics.detailedDescription: Measures whether a team's record was better or worse than their point differential suggests. Positive values indicate good luck, negative values indicate bad luck.
metrics.calculationFormula: Regular-Season Wins (ties as half) − Pythagorean Wins
metrics.exampleCalculation: Team with 10 actual wins and 8.2 expected wins: 10 - 8.2 = +1.8 (lucky)
metrics.interpretationGuide: Positive is lucky, negative unlucky. One season's standard deviation in this league is about 1.1 wins, so ±1.5 is a notable year and ±2.5 is rare. It does not persist: first-half luck predicts nothing about the second half (r = −0.04), and one season's luck nothing about the next (r = −0.09).
metrics.limitations: Measures only the gap between a record and its points; schedule luck (whom you drew in your best and worst weeks) and points luck (opponents having big weeks) are mixed together. Over a fourteen game season the spread is about one win, so a single season's value is weak evidence; a career total is more telling.

metrics.shortDescription: Difference in fantasy points produced between traded players
metrics.detailedDescription: Measures the net fantasy point gain/loss from a trade by comparing the production of players given away vs players received.
metrics.calculationFormula: Sum(Points of Players Received) - Sum(Points of Players Given Away)
metrics.exampleCalculation: Trade: Give RB (120 pts) + WR (80 pts), Get RB (150 pts): 150 - (120+80) = -50 points lost
metrics.interpretationGuide: Positive values favor the team, negative values favor the opponent. Values over ±50 points indicate significantly lopsided trades.
metrics.limitations: Counts only fantasy points produced after the trade. It ignores what each manager would otherwise have started, positional scarcity, and whether the player was even in the lineup, so points from a traded player who sat on a bench still count. Draft picks and FAAB included in a deal are not valued at all.

metrics.shortDescription: Which team got the better end of a trade based on production
metrics.detailedDescription: Determined by comparing the production differential and context scores. Accounts for playoff implications and team needs.
metrics.calculationFormula: Based on Production Differential, Playoff Impact, and Context Scores
metrics.exampleCalculation: Team A gets +30 points and makes playoffs: "Team A" wins the trade
metrics.interpretationGuide: Winners are determined by significant production advantages (25+ points) or crucial playoff implications.
metrics.limitations: Built on production differential, so it inherits its blind spots. The threshold for declaring a winner is a fixed point margin, which means trades near that line flip verdict on small scoring changes rather than on anything meaningful.

metrics.shortDescription: Players a manager brought onto their roster: free-agent adds, waiver claims and trades.
metrics.detailedDescription: Every transaction in league history where the player went to this manager. Moves per season spreads that total over the seasons they played.
metrics.calculationFormula: Total moves: every add, claim and trade that sent a player to this manager. Moves per season: total moves divided by seasons played.
metrics.exampleCalculation: A manager with 409 moves over 16 seasons: 409 ÷ 16 = 25.6 moves per season
metrics.interpretationGuide: More moves means a busier manager, not a better one. Read it next to FAAB efficiency to see whether the activity paid off.

metrics.shortDescription: How well a drafted player performed relative to their draft position
metrics.detailedDescription: Compares actual fantasy points to expected points based on draft position. Higher scores indicate better draft picks.
metrics.calculationFormula: Actual Fantasy Points ÷ Expected Points for Draft Position
metrics.exampleCalculation: Player drafted 30th overall scored 180 points (expected 120): 180÷120 = 1.50
metrics.interpretationGuide: 1.20+ is excellent value, 1.00-1.20 is good value, 0.80-1.00 is fair value, below 0.80 is poor value.
metrics.limitations: Expected points for a draft slot come from this league's own history, so the baseline moves whenever scoring settings change and the score is not comparable to public draft value figures. A player who is drafted and immediately injured scores near zero no matter how sound the pick was at the time.

metrics.shortDescription: Average fantasy points scored per week played
metrics.detailedDescription: Measures the weekly scoring rate for drafted players, accounting for games missed due to injury or benching.
metrics.calculationFormula: Total Fantasy Points ÷ Weeks Actually Played
metrics.exampleCalculation: Player with 180 total points in 12 weeks played: 180÷12 = 15.0 points per week
metrics.interpretationGuide: Position dependent: QB 18+, RB/WR 12+, TE 10+, K 8+, DEF 8+ are typically good weekly averages.
metrics.limitations: Divides by weeks actually played, so a player who missed most of a season can post an excellent rate off a handful of games. It is not position adjusted, which makes a quarterback and a kicker incomparable on this number alone.

metrics.shortDescription: A manager's career draft grade: how sure we can be that they draft better or worse than average.
metrics.detailedDescription: Each season's draft gets a score: its picks' points over what their positions and rounds usually score in this league, in average picks. The career grade divides a manager's average season score by its standard error, so one big year can't carry it. Most managers land on a C, which is the honest result when drafting skill is mostly noise.
metrics.calculationFormula: Average season draft score ÷ (spread of every finished season score ÷ √seasons). A at +2 or more, B at +0.75 or more, C within 0.75 either way, D down to -2, F below that.
metrics.exampleCalculation: A manager averaging +0.94 a season over 18 seasons, with a league spread of 3.0: 0.94 ÷ (3.0 ÷ √18) = 1.33, a B
metrics.interpretationGuide: Read it as how settled the record is, not how big it is. A B means a manager beats their slots season after season; a C means their seasons don't settle it either way.

metrics.shortDescription: How many average picks' worth of points a manager's drafts beat their slots by, per season.
metrics.detailedDescription: Every pick is judged against what players at the same position, taken around the same round, have scored in this league's finished seasons. A draft's value adds up its picks' points over that expectation and divides by what the season's average pick scored, so seasons with different scoring read on one scale. This is the average over a manager's finished seasons.
metrics.calculationFormula: For each finished season: the sum over the draft's picks of (points minus expected points), divided by the season's average pick. Then the average of those seasons.
metrics.exampleCalculation: A draft whose picks beat their slots by 280 points in a season where the average pick scored 140: 280 ÷ 140 = +2.0
metrics.interpretationGuide: 0 is an average draft. +1.0 is about one extra average pick's worth of points a year. Most managers sit within one of zero.

metrics.shortDescription: The share of a manager's picks that scored at least 80% of what their slot was expected to.
metrics.detailedDescription: A hit is any pick that came within 20% of what players at the same position, taken around the same round, have scored in this league, or beat it. Every pick counts, kickers and defenses included.
metrics.calculationFormula: Picks that scored at least 0.8 × their expected points ÷ all picks
metrics.exampleCalculation: 196 hits from 329 picks: 196 ÷ 329 = 60%
metrics.interpretationGuide: Most managers hit on 55% to 65% of their picks. A higher rate means fewer wasted picks, not bigger wins, so read it next to steals and busts.

metrics.shortDescription: Fantasy points scored above a replacement-level player at the same position
metrics.detailedDescription: Compares player production to the baseline production available on waivers. Higher values indicate more valuable players.
metrics.calculationFormula: Player Fantasy Points - Replacement Level Points for Position
metrics.exampleCalculation: RB scores 180 points when replacement level is 100: 180 - 100 = 80 points above replacement
metrics.interpretationGuide: 50+ is elite tier, 25-50 is very good, 0-25 is startable, negative values are below replacement level.
metrics.limitations: The replacement baseline is derived from this league's own waiver pool, so the values are not comparable to public VORP or PAR figures and shift with league size and roster requirements.

metrics.shortDescription: The share of 10,000 simulated seasons in which a team makes the playoffs.
metrics.detailedDescription: Multi-factor calculation considering current record, points scored, strength of schedule, and weeks remaining.
metrics.calculationFormula: Each team gets a projected score, pulled toward the league average early in the year. The rest of the season is played 10,000 times with that score drifting week to week, and seeds go by wins, then points for. A team's odds are the share of those runs where it makes the field.
metrics.interpretationGuide: 80%+ is very likely, 60-80% is likely, 40-60% is uncertain, 20-40% is unlikely, below 20% is very unlikely.
metrics.limitations: Not a simulation and not fitted. It is a hand-set ladder of rank, games back and week number. Backtested on 2005-2025 (2007 excluded, its bracket labels are unreliable) it beats simple baselines (Brier 0.159, against 0.213 for "in a playoff spot today") but is badly calibrated in the middle: teams given 40-50% made it 26% of the time, 70-80% made it 55%, 80-90% made it 73%. Odds across a league add to about 7.1 playoff spots in week 1 when there are 6, and do not settle to 0% or 100% by the final regular week.

categories.categoryDescription: Measures of performance consistency and reliability

metrics.shortDescription: Measures how consistent a manager's win rate is across different seasons
metrics.detailedDescription: Standard deviation of season win percentages. Lower values indicate more consistent performance year over year, while higher values suggest boom-or-bust seasons.
metrics.calculationFormula: Standard Deviation of (Season Win Percentages)
metrics.exampleCalculation: Manager with season win rates of 60%, 65%, 55%: StdDev = 5.0% (very consistent)
metrics.interpretationGuide: Lower is better. Observed league history spans 0.112 to 0.191, so read it relatively: below 0.130 is steady year to year, 0.130-0.170 is typical, above 0.170 is boom-or-bust.
metrics.limitations: Lower is better, which is the opposite direction to most metrics on this page. It is the standard deviation of weekly win percentage across a career rather than of season final records, so a manager with few seasons has an unstable value. It measures steadiness, not quality: a reliably poor manager scores as well as a reliably good one.

metrics.shortDescription: Standard deviation of weekly fantasy point totals
metrics.detailedDescription: Measures how predictable a player's weekly scoring is. Lower values indicate more consistent performers.
metrics.calculationFormula: Standard Deviation of Weekly Fantasy Points
metrics.exampleCalculation: Player with weekly scores of 12, 14, 11, 13: StdDev = 1.3 (very consistent)
metrics.interpretationGuide: Position dependent: Lower is better. QBs <3.0, RBs <4.0, WRs <5.0, TEs <4.0 are considered consistent.
metrics.limitations: Lower is better, which is the opposite direction to most metrics on this page. Weeks with zero points are dropped from the standard deviation, so a player who missed games looks steadier than he was. It is not scale free either: high scoring positions have larger deviations by construction, which is why the thresholds are position dependent.

metrics.shortDescription: Starter points produced by FAAB pickups, per FAAB dollar spent
metrics.detailedDescription: For every waiver claim a manager paid for, the fantasy points that player scored while in that manager's starting lineup, from the week of the claim until the same team claimed him again. Divided by the dollars spent. Bench weeks earn nothing: the question is what the money put in the lineup.
metrics.calculationFormula: Σ Starter Points from Paid Claims ÷ Σ FAAB Dollars Spent
metrics.exampleCalculation: $40 on a back who started 6 weeks for 72 points and $10 on a receiver who never started: (72 + 0) ÷ (40 + 10) = 1.44 points per dollar
metrics.interpretationGuide: Higher is better. Across this league (FAAB since 2022) it runs 0.21 to 3.13 with most managers near 1.5-2.1: above 2.5 is sharp bidding, below 1.0 is money left on the bench or the waiver wire.
metrics.limitations: Credits the whole of a player's starting production to the claim, with no allowance for who would otherwise have started, so it rewards claims that filled an empty slot as much as genuine upgrades. A player dropped and later re-added for free still credits the original paid claim. $0 claims are excluded because a rate per zero dollars is undefined, so a manager who wins players for nothing gets no credit here. Only 2022 onward: the league did not use FAAB before then.

metrics.shortDescription: Largest point differential in a single game victory
metrics.detailedDescription: The highest point difference achieved in any single game win.
metrics.calculationFormula: Winner Points - Loser Points (for victories only)
metrics.exampleCalculation: Team wins 145.2 to 78.4: Margin = 145.2 - 78.4 = 66.8 points
metrics.interpretationGuide: 50+ point wins are blowouts, 30-50 is decisive, 15-30 is solid, under 15 is close.
metrics.limitations: Only victories count. A manager's largest margin in a loss records as zero rather than as a negative, so this cannot be read as a general blowout tendency. One extreme game defines the value for an entire career.

metrics.shortDescription: Largest point differential in any head-to-head matchup
metrics.detailedDescription: The biggest blowout between any two managers in their historical matchups.
metrics.calculationFormula: Maximum of |Team A Points - Team B Points| across all games
metrics.exampleCalculation: Biggest blowout: 156.8 vs 67.2 = 89.6 point difference
metrics.interpretationGuide: 80+ is historically lopsided, 60-80 is very lopsided, 40-60 is lopsided, under 40 is competitive.
metrics.limitations: A single game extreme across the whole history, so it is driven by outliers and by how many times two managers happen to have played. It says nothing about the typical margin between them.

metrics.shortDescription: Measure of how active the waiver wire is in a league
metrics.detailedDescription: Calculated based on transaction frequency, FAAB usage, and player turnover rates.
metrics.calculationFormula: Based on transactions per team, FAAB utilization, and roster churn
metrics.exampleCalculation: League with 8 transactions/team/week, 80% FAAB used: High activity index
metrics.interpretationGuide: Higher values indicate more active management. Scales with league competitiveness and engagement.
metrics.limitations: Depends on transaction records, which are sparse or entirely absent for the earliest seasons. A low value in an old season may mean the data was never captured rather than that the league was quiet.
